header.scope: Lost: the international business went to local acquiring after Adyen's test; the US stayed with us.
header.tag_why: The deciding comparison was approval performance by country: Adyen's test on their international traffic returned results by country, while we answered with an average uplift and delivered his own market-by-market numbers three weeks late, after the test had finished.

trigger.insight: The evaluation began inside the account, not with a competitor: a new payments owner ran a decline analysis by country that we never saw and still can't reproduce. Our buyer left last year and the role he left was filled without our knowledge, so the first serious review of our performance in years was done without us.
trigger.messaging: Make a proactive per-market approvals review the default opener whenever a customer's payments owner changes, instead of relying on the global positioning in M1.

decider.insight: Stefan built the case and the CFO signed off, and we only know this because Stefan told us after it had happened. The transcript does not show that anyone from Stripe ever spoke to the CFO. Stefan's own words show that his test for proof was whether he could defend it to the CFO, and an average did not pass.
decider.messaging: Write acceptance claims so a payments lead can hand them straight to a CFO: their own markets, their own numbers, and the money involved, not a cross-customer average.

Her claim that developers love us and billing works is her own read, with no customer quote behind it, and it did not protect the international business.
message.messaging: Rewrite M4 so it leads with the customer's own approval rates and lift by market, and treat the average uplift as supporting context rather than the headline.

decided.insight: The rep's view that nothing could have been done doesn't hold up against her own account. Stefan asked for his market-by-market numbers, waited three weeks, and the test was over by the time they arrived. He later called that analysis the most useful thing we had sent him. His remark about hearing from Stripe only when he said he was leaving reads as the real turning point: our attention arrived too late. Whether the analysis reached him before or after the CFO approval is not established.
decided.messaging: Present Stripe's account coverage as someone checking your approvals before you ask, not a response that arrives once you threaten to leave.

gaps.insight: The gap was not an analysis we couldn't do. We could do it; it was slow and it wasn't routine. The second gap was a named person: M5 offers tiered response times, but Stefan wanted someone who looks at his numbers every month. Whether we can offer local acquiring in Brazil or the European markets he mentioned never came up, and the rep's admission that she wouldn't know what to pitch suggests she didn't know either.
gaps.messaging: Back M5 with a named owner who reviews the customer's approvals every month, and promise the per-market analysis on a turnaround that fits inside a competitor's test window.

language.insight: He framed the problem as money and ownership ('Money left on the table', 'what's mine'), and the mechanism as local infrastructure ('Local cards, local rails'). We framed it as product features ('Authorization Boost', 'Adaptive Acceptance', 'machine learning'). He says 'approvals' and we say 'authorization', so our words never matched the way he described the problem.
language.messaging: Use the customer's vocabulary in acceptance messaging: 'approvals', the money left on the table in your markets, and a direct answer to local cards and local rails.

close.rep_takeaway: When the person who bought from us leaves, treat the account as at risk, not healthy. Here a new head of payments was pulling declines by country while the account had gone roughly nine to ten months without a business review. The analysis that would have answered him existed and he called it the most useful thing we sent, but it landed three weeks after he asked. Get to the new owner early, bring his own approvals by market before he asks, and give him a name, so that 'I heard from Stripe when I said I was leaving' never becomes the story.
